en: Mahāniddesa,
Aṭṭhakavagga, 4.
Suddhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesa
Now he will explain the exposition of the Sutta on the Pure Octad:
"I see the pure, supreme, and healthy state;
through what is seen, a person attains complete purification."
Thus knowing and understanding that which is supreme, one attains the knowledge:
"I am pure, I am a pure observer. "I see the pure, the supreme, the healthy."
"I see the pure," thus I see the pure; "I perceive the pure," thus I perceive the pure; "I look upon the pure," thus I look upon the pure; "I contemplate the pure," thus I contemplate the pure;

"I examine the pure," thus I examine the pure. "The supreme health"—one who has attained supreme health, attained protection, attained a refuge, attained a shelter, attained fearlessness, attained the deathless, attained the nectar, attained Nibbāna—thus I see the pure, the supreme health.
“By what is seen, a person attains purification”:

through the seeing of forms by means of eye-consciousness, there is for a person purity, complete purity, and utter purity; liberation, complete liberation, and utter liberation. A person is purified, completely purified, and utterly purified; he is liberated, completely liberated, and utterly liberated.
Thus, “by what is seen, a person attains purification.”
"Knowing thus, having understood the supreme":
knowing thus, understanding, discerning, penetrating, and piercing through;

having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest that "this is the supreme, the foremost, the best, the distinguished, the preeminent, the highest, the most excellent"—thus it is said.
"Having known this as the supreme, he directly realizes it.
"One who contemplates purity is one who directly realizes through knowledge":

he who sees purity is one who contemplates purity; "directly realizes through knowledge" means that by seeing forms with eye-consciousness, one directly realizes it as knowledge, one directly realizes it as the path, one directly realizes it as the way, and one directly realizes it as the outlet.
One recognizes knowledge as the observer of purity.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“I see the pure, supreme, and healthy.”
A person’s purification comes through what is seen;
knowing this and understanding it as supreme,
one proceeds with the knowledge that "I am observing purity."
If a person’s purity comes through what is seen,
or if he abandons suffering through knowledge,
then that one who still possesses acquisitions is purified by something other [than the truth].
"For indeed, such a view leads him to ruin when he speaks thus:
'If purity comes to a man through what is seen.

If, by means of the seeing of forms with the eye-consciousness, there were for a man purity, purification, complete purification; liberation, release, complete release—if a man were thereby purified, cleansed, completely cleansed; liberated, released, completely released—"
If a person’s purity comes through what is seen,
or if they abandon suffering through knowledge— should a person, by means of visual consciousness and the seeing of forms,

abandon the suffering of birth, abandon the suffering of aging, abandon the suffering of illness, abandon the suffering of death, and abandon the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?— [this is not possible].
Or he abandons suffering through knowledge.

"He is purified by another [means], one who still possesses acquisitions"—by another means, that is, by an impure path, a wrong practice, a path that does not lead to liberation, other than the foundations of mindfulness; other than...

Apart from the right strivings, apart from the bases of psychic power, apart from the faculties, apart from the powers, apart from the factors of enlightenment, and apart from the noble eightfold path, a person is purified, cleansed, thoroughly cleansed; he is liberated, released, and completely released.
[Yet] one who still possesses the substrate of existence—one with lust, with hatred, with delusion, with conceit, with craving, with wrong view, with defilement, and with clinging—is thus described.
"One who still possesses acquisitions is purified by something else;
for views indeed defile him as he speaks thus.
It is that very view which defiles that person.
Thus this person is one of wrong view, of perverted vision.
"Speaking thus" means speaking, saying, declaring, illuminating, and expressing thus:
"The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. Speaking, saying, declaring, illuminating, and expressing thus.
“The world is eternal… the world is finite… the world is infinite…”
"The soul and the body are the same" … "the soul is one thing and the body another" … "a Tathāgata exists after death" …
“The Tathāgata does not exist after death… both exists and does not exist after death… neither exists nor does not exist after death;
this alone is the truth, all else is vain”— one who speaks thus, declares thus, says thus, elucidates thus, and expresses thus.
For such a person, their view indeed becomes a source of evil as they speak thus.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a man’s purity is thought to come from what he has seen..."
"Or he abandons suffering through knowledge;
he who still possesses acquisitions is purified by something else,
for such a speaker leads them into views."
A brahmin does not say that purity comes from anything else—
neither from what is seen, heard, moral conduct, vows, or what is sensed;
he is unstained by both merit and evil.
"One who has abandoned the self and does not perform [actions] here—such a one is a brahmin;
he does not say that purity comes from elsewhere, whether in what is seen, heard, in moral conduct and vows, or in what is sensed.
This is not a negation.
A “brahmin” is so called because he has banished seven things:

personality-belief has been banished; doubt has been banished; clinging to rules and observances has been banished; lust has been banished; hatred has been banished; delusion has been banished; and conceit has been banished.

Evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death have been banished from him.
Having cast off all evils, Sabhiya—
so said the Blessed One—
you are stainless, well-composed, and firm in self.
Having transcended saṃsāra, he is the absolute one;
unattached and such as he is, he is called a Brahmā.
A true Brahmin does not declare purification through anything else.

A brahmin [seeks] purity, purification, complete purification, and liberation by means of another, impure path, a wrong practice, a path that does not lead out, apart from the foundations of mindfulness,
apart from the right efforts, apart from the bases of psychic power, apart from the faculties, apart from the powers,
apart from the factors of enlightenment, and apart from the noble eightfold path.
"Regarding liberation and complete liberation, he does not say, nor speak, nor declare, nor illuminate, nor express [anything else]"—
thus the brahmin does not claim purity from anything else:
"In what is seen, heard, in moral habits and vows, or in what is sensed."
There are some ascetics and brahmins who seek purity through views.
They consider the sight of certain forms to be auspicious, and the sight of other forms to be inauspicious.
Of which forms do they consider the sight to be auspicious?
Emerging from that state at the appropriate time, they see forms associated with good omens:
they see a sparrow bird; they see a Phussa bamboo staff; they see a pregnant woman;
they see a man walking along with a child carried on his shoulder; they see a full water jar; they see a rohita fish.
They see a thoroughbred horse, they see a chariot drawn by a thoroughbred horse, they see a bull, they see a tawny cow.
They consider the sight of such forms to be auspicious.
Of what kinds of forms do they consider the sight to be inauspicious?
They see a heap of straw; they see a pot of buttermilk; they see an empty pot; they see an actor; they see a naked ascetic;
they see a donkey; they see a donkey-cart; they see a cart yoked to a single animal; they see one who is blind;
they see one who is maimed; they see one who is lame; they see one with a withered arm; they see one who is decrepit.
They see one who is sick, they see one who is dead;
they consider the sight of such forms to be inauspicious.
These are those recluses and brahmins who seek purity through views.
They declare that through what is seen there is purity, purification, complete purity, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation.
There are some recluses and brahmins who find purity in learning;
they declare that hearing certain sounds is auspicious, while hearing other sounds is inauspicious.
Of what sounds do they consider the hearing to be auspicious?
Having risen at the proper time, they hear sounds that have become auspicious:

"It increases," or "it is increasing," or "it is full," or "it is Phussa," or "it is Asoka," or "it is Sumanā," or "it is a favorable constellation," or "it is a favorable omen," or "it is glory," or "it is the increase of glory."
They consider the hearing of such sounds to be auspicious.
Of what sounds do they consider the hearing to be inauspicious? Such as:

"He is blind," or "He is withered," or "He is lame," or "He has a withered arm," or "He is decrepit," or "He is diseased," or "He is dead," or "They are cutting him," or "They are splitting him," or "They are burning him," or "He is lost," or "He is non-existent."
They consider the hearing of such sounds to be inauspicious.
These are those ascetics and brahmins who are purified by learning;
they consider purification, complete purification, total purification, liberation, complete liberation, and total liberation to be achieved through learning.
There are some recluses and brahmins who regard purity as being through virtue.

They claim that through mere virtue, mere restraint, mere self-control, and mere non-transgression, they have attained purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation.
The recluse Muṇḍikāputta speaks thus:
“Householder, I describe a person endowed with four qualities as one who has perfected the wholesome, who is supremely wholesome, who has attained the highest attainment, a recluse beyond reproach.
With which four?
Here, householder, one does not perform an evil deed with the body, does not utter evil speech, does not entertain evil intentions, and does not maintain an evil livelihood.”

“Householder, it is one endowed with these four qualities whom I describe as a person who has reached perfection in skill, the highest skill, and the ultimate attainment—the ascetic who is beyond reproach.

This being so, there are some ascetics and brahmins who regard purity through virtue; they claim that by mere virtue, mere restraint, mere self-control, and mere non-transgression, there is purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, release, and total release.
There are also some ascetics and brahmins who regard purity through vows.
They are either elephant-worshippers, or horse-worshippers, or cow-worshippers, or dog-worshippers,
or crow-worshippers, or Vāsudeva-worshippers, or Baladeva-worshippers, or Puṇṇabhadda-worshippers,
or Maṇibhadda-worshippers, or fire-worshippers, or Nāga-worshippers, or Supaṇṇa-worshippers.
Or they belong to the yakkhas, or they belong to the asuras, or they belong to the gandhabbas, or they belong to the great kings,
or they belong to the moon, or they belong to the sun, or they belong to Indra, or they belong to Brahmā,
or they belong to the gods, or they belong to the quarters of the sky.
These ascetics and brahmins are those purified by vows;
through their vows they claim purification, complete purification, total purification, liberation, complete liberation, and full liberation.
There are also some ascetics and brahmins who are purified by what is heard.
Rising from that state at the appropriate time, they touch the earth; they touch green grass,
they touch cow dung, they touch a tortoise, they tread upon a ploughshare, they touch a sesame carrier, they eat fragrant sesame,
they smear themselves with fragrant oil, they chew fragrant tooth-sticks, they bathe with fragrant clay, and they wear fragrant garments.
They wrap themselves in a turban of cloth.
These are those recluses and brahmins who are purified by what is spun;
they declare that through what is spun there is purity, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total release.
The brahmin does not say that purity comes from anything else—
whether from what is seen, heard, moral conduct, vows, or what is sensed.
The brahmin does not say that purity comes from purity of what is seen, nor does he say that purity comes from purity of what is heard, nor does he say that purity comes from purity of moral conduct.

"I do not say purity through the purification of vows; I do not say purity through the purification of what is heard; I do not say purity through the purification of what is sensed—I do not speak it, do not utter it, do not illuminate it, do not declare it"—thus, "a brahmin does not say that purity comes from anything else:
whether from what is seen, what is heard, virtuous conduct and vows, or what is sensed."
"Unstained by merit and demerit. Merit is said to be any wholesome volitional formation pertaining to the three realms; demerit is said to be all that is unwholesome.

When the volitional formation of merit, the volitional formation of demerit, and the volitional formation of the imperturbable have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future;

"To this extent, one is not smeared by merit or evil, not defiled, not stained; unsmeared, undefiled, unstained, gone forth, escaped, liberated, dissociated, one dwells with a mind that has transcended all boundaries—thus, 'unsmeared by merit and evil.
Having abandoned self, one does nothing more here."
He has abandoned the self; he has abandoned the view of self. He has abandoned the self;

he has abandoned the grasping. Whatever was grasped, adhered to, clung to, obsessed over, and intent upon by way of craving and by way of views—all that has been relinquished, vomited out, released, forsaken, and cast away.

"Not performing here" means not performing, not generating, not producing, not bringing forth, and not causing the manifestation of either a meritorious formation, a non-meritorious formation, or an imperturbable formation—
one who has abandoned the self does not perform here.
Thus the Blessed One said:
“The Brahmin does not say that purity comes from anything else—
neither from what is seen, heard, moral conduct, vows, or what is sensed;
he is unsmeared by both merit and evil.”
“One who has abandoned the self does not act here [for its sake].
Those who, having abandoned the former, cling to the latter, follow after the urge of craving; they do not cross over attachment.
They grasp and then let go, like a monkey letting go of one branch while grasping another;
having abandoned the former, it clings to the latter.
Having abandoned their former teacher, they rely on another teacher;
having abandoned the former teaching of the Dhamma, they rely on another teaching of the Dhamma;
having abandoned their former community, they rely on another community.
Having abandoned the former view, they rely on another view;
having abandoned the former practice, they rely on another practice;
having abandoned the former path, they rely on another path—they are dependent, attached, clinging, drawn near, infatuated, and intent upon it.
Having abandoned the former, they cling to the latter;
following after craving, they do not cross over but remain entangled.
Craving is called *ejā*.
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness;

those who follow after craving, who are pursued by craving, who have followed after craving, who have been assailed by craving, who have fallen into craving, who are overwhelmed by craving, whose minds are consumed by craving—they do not cross over, they are stuck in the attachment of lust, the attachment of hatred, the attachment of delusion, the attachment of conceit, the attachment of views, and the attachment of the defilements.
"They do not cross over, they do not emerge, they do not leap across, they do not transcend, they do not go beyond the attachment to misconduct"— thus,
"those who follow craving do not cross over the attachment.
They "take up and let go" means they take up one teacher, and having released him, they take up another teacher.
They take up one teaching of the Dhamma and, having abandoned it, take up another teaching of the Dhamma;
they join one group and, having abandoned it, join another group;
they adopt one view and, having abandoned it, adopt another view.
They take up a practice and, letting that go, they take up another practice;
they take up a path and, letting that go, they take up another path;
they both take up and let go, both adopt and relinquish.
They take up [the thought] and let it go.
"Like a monkey letting go of and seizing a branch":
just as a monkey wandering through a forest grove seizes a branch, and having released that, seizes another branch.
In the same way, many recluses and brahmins grasp and let go of, take up and cast aside, various speculative views— just as a monkey,
letting go of one branch, seizes another.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Abandoning the former and clinging to the latter,
those who follow after craving do not cross over attachment.
They grasp and then let go;”
“Just as a monkey, letting go of one branch, seizes another.
A person who has undertaken various vows,
being bound by perceptions, goes from one state to another.
The wise one, having understood the Dhamma through the Vedas and having realized it for himself,
does not fall into high and low states, he of vast wisdom;
for he has personally undertaken the vows, O people.
"Having undertaken by oneself" means having undertaken it personally.
"Vows" refers to the elephant-vow, the horse-vow, the cow-vow, the cock-vow, the crow-vow, the Vāsudeva-vow,
the Baladeva-vow, the Puṇṇabhadda-vow, the Maṇibhadda-vow, the fire-vow, or the Nāga-vow.

Or having taken up, undertaken, adopted, embraced, grasped, clung to, and adhered to the observance of the *supaṇṇas*, or the observance of the *yakkhas*, or the observance of the *asuras* …pe… or the observance of the *disās*.
"A creature" means a being, a person …pe… a human being.
A person who has undertaken various vows goes from one teacher to another teacher,
and from one teaching of the Dhamma to another teaching of the Dhamma, being a being driven by perceptions.
He goes from group to group;
he goes from view to view;
he goes from practice to practice.
He goes from path to path.
"Attached by perception" means he is attached, bound up, clinging, stuck, held fast, and obstructed by sensual perception, ill-will perception, cruelty perception, and views-perception.
It is just as goods placed on a wooden post or a peg are attached, bound up, clinging, stuck, held fast, and obstructed.

Just as a tree stump is obstructed, so too, one who is a being, attached, clinging, bound, fettered, and obstructed by perceptions of sensual desire, perceptions of ill will, perceptions of cruelty, and perceptions of views,
wanders up and down, bound by perceptions.
"And having understood the Dhamma through the Vedas.
Here, "the wise one" (*vidvā*) means one who is wise, possessed of true knowledge (*vijjā*), a knower, one of clear vision, and intelligent. "Through the Vedas" (*vedehi*):

the "Vedas" refers to the knowledge of the four paths; it is wisdom (*paññā*), the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*), the power of wisdom (*paññābala*), the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*), inquiry (*vīmaṃsā*), insight (*vipassanā*), and right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).
By those knowledges, he has reached the end of birth, aging, and death; he has attained the end, reached the limit, attained the limit,
gone to the boundary, attained the boundary, gone to the finality, attained the finality, gone to refuge, attained refuge, gone to shelter, attained shelter,
gone to protection, attained protection, gone to fearlessness, attained fearlessness, gone to the deathless, attained the deathless, and reached the state of the immortal.
He has reached the deathless, gone to Nibbāna, attained Nibbāna.

Or, he is a "Vedagū" because he has reached the end of feelings; or he is a "Vedagū" because he has reached the end by means of knowledge; or he is a "Vedagū" because of his having understood seven things.
The view of a personal body has been understood, doubt has been understood, and adherence to rules and observances has been understood.
Lust is known, hatred is known, delusion is known, conceit is known;
evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, provocative of trouble, resulting in suffering, and conducive to future birth, aging, and death, are known by him.
Having thoroughly examined all the Vedas, he has understood them completely.
(To Sabhiya, the Blessed One said:
"Whatever [qualities] belong to recluses and brahmins,
[I am] free from passion toward all feelings."
"He is a knower of the Vedas, having transcended all Vedic knowledge.
And: "The wise one, having fully understood the Dhamma through the Vedas. Having fully understood, having thoroughly realized the Dhamma.
Having fully understood and realized the Dhamma that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent";
having fully understood and realized the Dhamma that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering";
having fully understood and realized the Dhamma that "all phenomena are non-self."
Having fully understood and realized the Dhamma: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise";
having fully understood and realized the Dhamma: "With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises";
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises...
With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with contact as condition, feeling arises.
With feeling as condition, craving arises;
with craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises.
Having fully understood and realized the Dhamma: "With existence as condition, there is birth" ... "With birth as condition, there is aging and death";
and having fully understood and realized the Dhamma: "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations."
Having fully understood and realized the Dhamma: "With the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness";
"with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form";
"with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases."
With the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact...
with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling...
with the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving...
With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging... with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence...
with the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth...
Having fully understood and realized the Dhamma that with the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death;
having fully understood and realized the Dhamma that "this is suffering"; [having fully understood and realized the Dhamma that] "this is the origin of suffering"...
Having fully understood and realized the Dhamma: "This is the cessation of suffering"; having fully understood and realized the Dhamma: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering";
having fully understood and realized the Dhamma: "These are the taints."
"This is the origin of the taints," "this is the cessation of the taints," and "this is the way leading to the cessation of the taints"— having thus fully understood and realized the Dhamma.
"These phenomena are to be directly known"—having thus fully understood and realized the Dhamma;
"these phenomena are to be fully understood"...
"these phenomena are to be abandoned"... [and so forth].
"Having fully understood and realized the Dhamma that 'these phenomena are to be developed'... having fully understood and realized the Dhamma that 'these phenomena are to be realized.
Having fully understood and realized the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact, one has realized the Dhamma."
Having fully understood and realized the Dhamma regarding the arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape from the five aggregates subject to clinging;
having fully understood and realized the Dhamma regarding the arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape from the four great elements;
and having fully understood and realized the Dhamma that "whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation"—this is called the Dhamma.
And the wise one, having understood the Dhamma through the Vedas,
does not go from high to low— that is, he does not go from teacher to teacher,
from teaching of the Dhamma to teaching of the Dhamma, from group to group, or from view to view— being one of vast wisdom.
He goes from way to way, not from path to path.
"Of vast wisdom" means he is one of vast wisdom, great wisdom, wide wisdom, laughing wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom.
"Vast" (bhūri) is said to be the earth.
"Endowed with that wisdom which is equal to the earth, vast and extensive—
one of broad wisdom does not go from high to low.
Thus said the Blessed One.
“A person who has undertaken various vows,
being bound by perceptions, goes from one state to another;
but the wise one, having understood the Dhamma through his knowledge, [remains steadfast].”
"One of vast wisdom does not go to high and low states.
He has become free from enmity toward all phenomena—
whatever is seen, heard, or sensed.
Who here in the world could form a conceptual construction about that very one who sees and moves about with open eyes?
He has become free from enmity toward all phenomena— whatever is seen, heard, or sensed.
"Army" refers to Māra’s army. Bodily misconduct is Māra’s army; verbal misconduct is Māra’s army; mental misconduct is Māra’s army; lust is Māra’s army; hatred is Māra’s army;
delusion is Māra’s army; anger is Māra’s army; resentment ... [and so on] ... all unwholesome volitional formations are Māra’s army.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Sensual pleasures are your first army;
the second is called discontent.”
The third is hunger and thirst for you;
the fourth is called craving.
The fifth is sloth and torpor for you.
The sixth is said to be cowardice;
the seventh is doubt for you,
and the eighth is hypocrisy and obstinacy.
Gain, fame, and honor,
and whatever reputation is wrongly acquired;
whoever exalts himself—
And others he despises.
This is your army, O Namuci,
the assailant of Kaṇha.
“No hero conquers him;
having conquered, he obtains happiness.

When, by means of the four noble paths, the entire army of Māra and all the defilements that act as adversaries have been conquered, defeated, broken, shattered, and turned away, he is called “one who has become free from the enemy host.”
Thus, being detached from what is seen, detached from what is heard, detached from what is sensed, and detached from what is cognized— he is detached from all phenomena,
whatever is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. Such a one is called "one who sees,
walking with the doors of perception open."
One who sees that very [truth]—one with pure vision, purified vision, completely purified vision, bright vision, and thoroughly cleansed vision;
or alternatively, one whose vision is pure, whose vision is purified, whose vision is completely purified, whose vision is bright, and whose vision is thoroughly cleansed.
"Opened" means the covering of craving, the covering of views, the covering of defilements, the covering of misconduct, and the covering of ignorance have been removed.
Those coverings are opened up, shattered, uncovered, utterly removed, abandoned, cut off, stilled, calmed, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt away by the fire of knowledge.
"Wandering" means wandering, roaming, dwelling, moving about, acting, maintaining, sustaining, and carrying on—
that very seer wandering with [all] doors open.
"How could one form a conceptualization regarding this world?
"Conceptualizations" (kappa) are two types:
the conceptualization of craving (taṇhākappa) and the conceptualization of views (diṭṭhikappa)... [and so forth]...
This is the construction of craving... [as before] ...this is the construction of views.
His construction of craving has been abandoned; his construction of views has been relinquished.
Because the construction of craving has been abandoned and the construction of views has been relinquished, by what passion would one construct?
By what hatred would one construct? By what delusion would one construct? By what conceit would one construct? By what view would one construct?
By what restlessness would one construct? By what doubt would one construct? By what underlying tendencies would one construct?
Whether as "lustful," or "hated," or "deluded," or "bound," or "misapprehended," or "distracted," or "gone astray," or "become habitual"—
those volitional formations have been abandoned.
Because volitional formations have been abandoned, by what means could one be reckoned to any state of existence?
Whether one is a denizen of hell, or of the animal realm, or of the sphere of hungry ghosts, or a human, or a deva; whether one is possessed of form, or formless;

whether one is percipient, or non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—there is no cause, no condition, no reason by which one could conceive, could differentiate, or could fall into such conceptualization.
"In the world" means: in the world of the states of misery, the world of humans, the world of devas, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases.
Who in this world could form a conceptual construction about him?
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"He has become free from enmity toward all phenomena..."
Whatever has been seen, heard, or sensed—
seeing only that, wandering with an open mind,
whom in this world could one find to dispute?
They do not construct [views], nor do they hold them as foremost;
they do not say, "This is absolute purity.
Having released the knot of grasping that binds them fast,
They do not form any hope anywhere in the world;
they do not construct [conceptual fabrications] and do not hold them as foremost.
"Constructing" (kappa) refers to two kinds of constructing:
The conceptualization of craving and the conceptualization of views...
[as follows] ...this is the conceptualization of craving... [as follows] ...this is the conceptualization of views.
For them, the construction of craving has been abandoned, and the construction of views has been relinquished.

Because the construction of craving has been abandoned and the construction of views has been relinquished, they do not construct, do not generate, do not produce, do not bring about, and do not cause to arise either the construction of craving or the construction of views; thus, "they do not construct."
“They do not hold in high esteem.
There are two kinds of esteem:
esteem based on craving and esteem based on views... [etc. ...
This is prioritizing craving... [and so on] ...this is prioritizing views.
Among them, prioritizing craving has been abandoned; prioritizing views has been relinquished.

Because craving has been abandoned as their primary concern and views have been relinquished as their primary concern, they do not go about making either craving or views their forerunners; they do not have craving as their banner, craving as their standard, or craving as their overlord;
they do not have views as their banner, views as their standard, or views as their overlord; and they do not go about surrounded by either craving or views.
“They do not construct [theories], they do not hold [them] foremost.

‘They do not say there is ultimate purity’ means: they do not say, do not speak, do not utter, do not illuminate, and do not declare that there is ultimate purity—that is, purity from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), the view of non-action (*akriyā-dṛṣṭi*), or the doctrine of eternalism (*sassata-vāda*)—thus, ‘they do not say there is ultimate purity.’”
He releases the knot of grasping that was tied.
"Knots" refers to the four knots:
the bodily knot of covetousness, the bodily knot of ill will, the bodily knot of adherence to rules and observances, and the bodily knot of dogmatic insistence on "this alone is the truth."
Attachment to one’s own view is the bodily tie of covetousness;
resentment toward the doctrines of others is the bodily tie of ill will;

clinging to one’s own morality, vows, or moral-vow observances is the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances; and the insistence that “one’s own view alone is the truth” is the bodily tie of dogmatic adherence.
For what reason is it called the "bond of grasping"?
Because by means of those bonds they grasp at, cling to, seize, misapprehend, and adhere to form;
[they do the same with] feeling...
perception … volitional formations … consciousness …
… destiny … rebirth … relinking …
They take up, cling to, grasp, misapprehend, and adhere to existence... and the cycle of saṃsāra.
For that reason, it is called the "fetter of grasping."
"Having released from the bonds (*visajja*)," that is, having cast off the bonds. Alternatively,

having shaken loose the bonds— that is, the clinging, the entanglement, the binding, the obstruction, the fettering, the sticking, the being stuck, the being impeded, and the bond— once they have been loosened.
Having unyoked.
Just as they unyoke, dismantle, and disassemble a draft animal, a chariot, a cart, or a carriage;
even so, having cast off the bonds—
Having released.

Or alternatively: having loosened the knots, the entanglements, the bonds, the obstructions, the fetters, the attachments, the clingings, the hindrances, the ties, and the shackles, he releases—the grasping-knot that was knotted, he releases.
They do not form any expectation regarding anything in the world.
"Expectation" is said to be craving—that which is lust, infatuation... [as above] ...covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
"They do not form an expectation" means they do not form it, do not produce it, do not generate it, do not bring it into being, do not cause it to arise.
“Anywhere” means anywhere, in anything, in any place—whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally.
“In the world” refers to the world of the lower realms (*apāyaloka*) … [and so on] … up to the world of the sense bases (*āyatanaloka*).
They do not form any expectation regarding anything in the world.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“They do not construct mental fabrications, nor do they hold them as foremost;
they do not say, ‘This is absolute purity.’”
Having relinquished the knot of grasping that binds, they form no expectations anywhere in the world.
For such a one, there is no boundary; he is a brahmin who has transcended all limits.
Having known or having seen what was grasped,
he is neither one who clings with passion nor one who delights in dispassion;
for him, there is nothing here that is further grasped.
"The brahmin has transcended the boundary; for him there is nothing grasped through knowing or seeing.
"Boundary" refers to four boundaries:

the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*), the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*), and the defilements associated with them.
This is the first boundary.
Gross fetters of sensual lust and aversion, the gross underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion, and the defilements associated with them—
this is the second boundary.

The fetter of sensual lust that is present as a residual tendency, the fetter of aversion, the underlying tendency to sensual lust that is present as a residual tendency, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the defilements associated therewith—this is the third boundary.

Sense-sphere lust, fine-material lust, immaterial lust, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance; the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, the underlying tendency to ignorance, and the defilements associated therewith—[this is the fourth boundary].
This is the fourth boundary.
And when one has transcended, surpassed, and passed beyond these four boundaries by means of the four noble paths, he is called "one who has transcended the boundaries.
He is a brahmin because of having banished seven things.
The view of a personal body has been expelled, doubt has been expelled, and clinging to rules and observances has been expelled...
[as before] ...he is called unattached and such-like; he is a Brahmā.
"Of him" means of the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"Having known" means having known either by means of the knowledge of others' minds or by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
"Having seen" means having seen either with the fleshly eye or with the divine eye.
For that brahmin who has transcended the boundary, there is nothing [further] to be grasped, whether through knowing or through seeing.
Regarding this, there is nothing that is supreme, foremost, best, distinguished, preeminent, highest, or most excellent— which has been grasped, clung to, adhered to, obsessed over, and intent upon—
that does not exist, is not present, is not found, and is not obtainable; for it has been abandoned,
cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
The brahmin has transcended the boundary; for him there is nothing grasped through knowing or seeing.
He is neither one who lusts after passion nor one stained by the fading of passion.
Those "stained by passion" are said to be those who are attached, greedy, infatuated, obsessed, clinging, clung to, and obstructed by the five strands of sensual pleasure.

Those who are "attached to dispassion" (*virāgaratta*) are said to be those who are attached, greedy, infatuated, obsessed, clinging, stuck, and bound to the meditative attainments of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*).

One is "neither lustful with lust nor attached to dispassion" when sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), form-lust (*rūparāga*), and formless-lust (*arūparāga*) have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future.
To this extent one is neither lustful with lust nor attached to dispassion.
"Of him, here, there is nothing further to be grasped.
"Of him" means of the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"Of him" refers to that which has been grasped, clung to, as supreme, foremost, best, distinguished, preeminent, highest, and most excellent.
That which was adhered to, clung to, and devoted to—does not exist, is not present, is not found, and is not obtained;
it has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided; it is incapable of arising again, being burnt by the fire of knowledge—thus, for him, there is nothing here that is grasped as supreme.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The Brahmin has transcended all limits;
for him there is nothing grasped through knowing or seeing.”
Neither passionate with passion nor attached to dispassion—
for him, there is nothing here that is grasped as supreme.
This concludes the fourth exposition, the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta.
